title.narrative: Bangladesh Third Programmatic Jobs Development Policy Credit

description.narrative: The Bangladesh Jobs DPC supports the Government of Bangladesh's program of reforms to address the country's jobs challenges by: (i)modernizing the trade and investment environment; (ii) strengthening systems that protect workers and build resilience; and (iii) improving policies and programs that enhance access to jobs for vulnerable populations

The development objectives of the Third Programmatic Jobs Development Policy Credit Project in Bangladesh address the country's jobs challenges by: (i) modernizing the trade and investment environment; (ii) strengthening systems that protect workers and build resilience; and (iii) improving policies and programs that enhance access to jobs for vulnerable populations. The program includes the following pillars. Pillar A: modernizing the trade and investment environment, lays the foundation for continued progress towards upper middle-income status. Bangladesh has achieved remarkable growth through integration in the ready-made garment global value chain. However, exports remain heavily concentrated in the RMG sector, which accounted for approximately 83 percent of all exports in FY20. Pillar A supports job creation and the COVID-19 recovery by strengthening the investment climate, promoting exports, and helping mitigate environmental and climate change impacts of industrial expansion. These four actions will be particularly important to help Bangladesh sustain recovery momentum as global demand picks up. Pillar B: Strengthening systems that protect workers and build resilience, focuses on increasing protection of Bangladeshi workers, It includes policy actions to strengthen the Government of Bangladesh's (GoB's) capacity to respond to the COVID-19 crisis and future crises, and supports: (i) job quality through interventions protecting the earnings of workers affected by the COVID19 crisis; (ii) GoB's mechanisms to coordinate response to shocks and deploy safety net programs; and (iii) GoB's capacity to enforce labor regulations and standards that expand workers protection. Pillar C: improving policies and programs to enhance access to jobs for vulnerable populations, supports key policies to strengthen programs and institutions that help youth, women, and overseas migrants access job opportunities. The COVID-19 crisis has further exacerbated the need for interventions which promote economic inclusion for women, youth, and migrants.

title.narrative: # of competency standards (by occupation and level) developed and introduced in at least one training center

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result Indicator 14 was over-achieved</strong>, with a total of 569 (of which 464 prepared by the BTEB and 105 by the NSDA) competency standards developed (against a target of 500), and 10 additional competency standards currently under development. These competency standards are common goods to be used across the sector by all actors, which can be developed by different relevant government agencies.</p>

title.narrative: Annual growth in new business registrations (disaggregated by gender)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator 2 is considered achieved even though a sub-indicator is not measurable. </strong>For this indicator, the target was also surpassed with a growth in the number of new business registration of 14.9% per annum (versus an initial target of 5% per annum). While gender disaggregated data is not available, one could reasonably confidently assume that the initial target of 10% per annum for women was achieved, since the overall result was 14.9% (for men and women combined). ???????</p>

title.narrative: Number of active bond license holders outside RMG sector

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator 5 target was largely exceeded, despite the pandemic. </strong>Overall, this demonstrates the important progress made, notably to open the regime to sectors beyond the RMG sector. It also demonstrates the importance of parallel technical support from IFC to implement the reform.</p>

title.narrative: "# of workers trained in partnership with private industries with support from the NSDA/Industry Skills Councils (by gender) "

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator 13 is not achieved</strong>. Progress in the Result indicator 13 on the number of workers trained was on track until March 2020, when all training were suspended due to the pandemic (the overall number of men trained was 88 percent of the target, while the number of women trained by March 2020 was 57 percent of the target).</p>

title.narrative: Budget allocation for supporting the protection of expatriate workers

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator 12 target is achieved</strong>. the indicator was calculated on the basis of the WEWB actual expenditures and captures greater fee collection from migrants rather than an increase in the Government’s financial engagement. The initial formulation in DPC1 was clearer (“Budget allocation for legal assistance for expatriate workers and emergency repatriation of female workers”) but too narrow to capture the range of services provided. All services were therefore includedstarting with DPC2 (such as “financial assistance for medical expenses”, “disabled/injured worker repatriation”, and “Repatriation of workers stuck abroad due to COVID-19”. </p>

title.narrative: Average cost of migration through formal channels (disaggregated by gender)

target.value: BDT 313,841 (male); BDT 189,809 (female) in 2018 Taka - inflation adjusted [25% reduction]

comment.narrative:
<p><strong>Result indicator 11 target was partially achieved</strong>, as average migration costs for women were reduced by 65percent, but costs for men increased by 1 percent. Two factors contributed: (i) most female migration during this period was domestic workers (84%) who have the lowest earnings among all migrants; and (ii) Saudi Arabia was the destination country for most female migrants (53%) and has the lowest average migration cost, reflecting a lag effect from the bilateral agreement signed between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia in February 2015.</p>

<p>The costs for male were expected to decrease as a result of the regulation of recruitment agencies, which has yet to be fully implemented, and a suspension of all outmigration during the COVID crisis has led to a halt in the processing (and hence application of new rules).</p>

title.narrative: Total of ministry budgets allocated to climate change capacity building and institutional strengthening

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator 6 exceeded the target</strong>. Based on the information available in the “Climate Financingfor Sustainable Development: Budget Report 2021-22”, the indicator has achieved 171% of the targeted increase of 10% per annum on average between FY19 to FY22.</p>

<p><strong>Customs inspections and clearance time RIs were relevant and appropriate. </strong>While RI-3 has achieved its target, RI-4 has not. Available information from World Customs Organization’s Time Release Study 2022 suggests that average import clearance time increased from the baseline for both Chittagong and Dhaka. The increase in customs clearance time is partially attributable to a significant increase in import volumes and substantial port congestion during the final reporting period. A new IPF is supporting customs modernization in Chittagong.</p>

title.narrative: Licensing and regulatory framework for child daycare centers adopted for use

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator 15<strong> </strong>is considered as not having met its target</strong>, although the rules for its operationalization and the licensing and regulatory framework for child daycare centers are currently being developed and are expected to be adopted by end 2022. A more thorough analysis of political economy and capacity constraints could have helped to better assess the reform feasibility and identify areas where technical assistance could have contribute to a speedier implementation.</p>

title.narrative: Adoption of national disaster risk management strategy that strengthens government coordination for climate resilience and disaster risk management

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator 9 target is achieved</strong>. MoDMR revised the previous disaster risk management strategy (NPDM 2016-2020) and developed a draft in November 2020. The draft was then approved in January 2021 as the “National Plan for Disaster Management (NDMP) 2021-2025”. The NDMP 2021-2025 is currently operational and being implemented by MoDMR.</p>

title.narrative: Time to and cost to set up a new business (disaggregated by gender)

baseline.value: Time: 19.5 days; Cost: 22.3% of income/capita (no gender difference)

target.value: Time: 14.6 days (25% reduction); Cost: 16.7% of income/capita (25% reduction)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator 1 targets were largely exceeded. </strong>For indicator 1, the time needed to set up a business was reduced from 19.5 days to 9.5 days (target was set at 14.6 days), so the reduction was twice as much as the target). The reduction in time to setup a new business was mainly driven by (i) reduced number of steps to set up a business from 9 to 6 (–1 day), (ii) partial automation of trade license process (–4 days), and (iii) automation of VAT registration process (–5 days). Streamlining and automation of business registration processes resulted in cost reduction from 22.3% of income per capita to 7.1% of income per capita, against a target of 16.7% (driven both by a reduction in absolute cost and by an increase in Bangladesh’s per-capita income).???????</p>

title.narrative: Number of firms reached through trainings/assessments of ESQ and OSH guidelines

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator 7 is considered as achieved</strong>, with a total of 1,340 firms/individuals assessed or trained. However, the indicator lacked specification since assessments are counted by firms while trainings are counted by individuals. Establishing two separate targets for trainings (number of individuals trained) and assessments (number of firms assessed) would have been more appropriate.</p>

title.narrative: Number of individuals supported by COVID-19 response programs

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator 8 largely exceeded the target</strong>. The Number of individuals supported by COVID-19 response programs stood at 7.6 million, including 3.8 million (wage support for export industry workers program), 3.5 million (cash transfer for informal workers program); 9,000 (support for the destitute export-oriented RMG and leather sector program); and 0.33 million (PKSF LRL program) as of April 2022.</p>
